task_title: Radio Communications, Navigation Systems/Facilities, and Radar Services
objective: By the end of this lesson you can keep the airplane under control by instruments while you tune and identify radios, follow a VOR or GPS course, talk to ATC correctly, follow their instructions, and know when to ask for help.
why: If you ever lose the horizon, ATC and your nav radios are your way out, but only if you can use them without losing control of the airplane.

prereading.what: Com radios, audio panel, transponder, communication procedures, FSS, tower, TRACON, ARTCC.
prereading.label: IFH Ch 2, 2-1 to 2-7

prereading.what: VOR receiver, CDI, TO/FROM, HSI, tracking, course interception, VOR errors.
prereading.label: IFH 9-10 to 9-15

prereading.what: Radio technique, initial contact, acknowledging frequency changes, call signs.
prereading.label: AIM 4-2-1 to 4-2-4

prereading.what: Safety alerts, radar assistance to VFR aircraft, basic radar service.
prereading.label: AIM 4-1-16 to 4-1-18

prereading.what: Ask for help early; help for VFR aircraft in difficulty.
prereading.label: AIM 6-1-2, 6-2-1

warmup: Under the hood, ATC says: "Cessna 12345, turn left heading 270, contact Approach on 124.35." What do you do first: turn, read back, or change the frequency?

key_terms.def: The radio transmits and receives on the active frequency; you preset the next one in standby and swap.
Selects which radio you transmit on and which radios you hear.
Repeating ATC's numbers (altitudes, headings, runways) to confirm you heard them right.
Course selector knob and the left-right needle that shows where the selected course is.
Horizontal situation indicator: heading indicator and CDI in one instrument.
Approach control (terminal radar) and Center (en route radar) facilities.
Transponder button that makes your target stand out on the controller's screen.
PAN-PAN: in trouble but not yet in immediate danger. MAYDAY: in serious, immediate danger.

body.p: You talk to ATC on VHF frequencies from 118.000 to 136.975 MHz. You need 25 kHz spacing (like 134.575) for full use of the system. If ATC gives you a frequency your radio can't select, ask for another one [[23:53|IFH 2-2]].

bullets: Many radios hold one active frequency and one or more stored in standby [[23:53|IFH 2-2]].
The audio panel sets volume, picks the transmitter, and picks speaker or headphones [[23:53|IFH 2-2]].
Switching the transmitter between COM1 and COM2 changes both what you send and hear. Use it to listen to ATIS on one radio while you work ATC on the other [[23:54|IFH 2-3]].
Use a headset with a boom mic close to your lips. A hand mic means reaching and hanging it up, a distraction [[23:53|IFH 2-2]].
Some GPS-com units can pick the right com frequency for you as you cross an airspace boundary or fix [[23:54|IFH 2-3]].

body.p: On a glass panel, the same radios live on the PFD and MFD bezels: NAV and COM frequency windows, NAV and COM knobs, and the audio panel between the screens [[23:153|IFH 6-20]].

callout.text: Trim first. A trimmed airplane lets you take your eyes off the attitude indicator for a moment to tune a radio without drifting [[23:153|IFH 6-20]]. Tune in short glances, then back to the scan.

check.q: ATC assigns a frequency your radio can't tune. What do you do?
check.a: Ask ATC for an alternative frequency [[23:53|IFH 2-2]].

chunks.title: Talking to ATC and following instructions

body.p: Understanding is the single most important thing. Be brief, but use whatever words it takes [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1]].

bullets: Listen before you transmit. After changing frequency, pause and listen [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]].
Think before you key the mic. Know what you'll say [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]].
Initial call: facility name, your full call sign, then your request or type of message [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3]]. Example: "Miami Center, Baron Five Six Three Hotel, request V-F-R traffic advisories."
Acknowledge frequency changes before switching; otherwise the controller can't tell if you heard it or lost your radio [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3]].
Change frequency as soon as possible unless told to change at a time, fix or altitude [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3]].
Don't abbreviate your call sign on initial contact or when similar call signs are on frequency [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]].

body.p: Read back altitudes, vectors (headings) and runway assignments, in the order given, with your call sign [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]] [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]]. Example: "Climbing to Flight Level three three zero, United Twelve." [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]]

callout.text: Except in an emergency, no one may operate contrary to an ATC instruction where ATC is exercised. If you are unsure of a clearance, ask right away [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123]]. You may refuse a clearance you can't safely fly; accepting it is your call [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]].

body.p: Tips: write down long clearances; the IFH has a shorthand (for example, RH = runway heading, SQ = squawk) [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]] [[23:340|IFH A-1]] [[23:341|IFH A-2]]. If no one answers, check volume, frequency, and that your mic isn't stuck on [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]].

callout.text: Under the hood: Fly first (start the turn or climb), then read back, then change frequency. A short delay on the readback is better than losing control.

check.q: Which parts of an instruction must you read back?
check.a: Altitude assignments, vectors and runway assignments, with your call sign [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]].

chunks.title: Navigation displays: VOR, HSI and GPS

body.p: VOR frequencies are 108.0 to 117.95 MHz. Turn up the volume and listen to the station identifier before relying on it [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].

head: VOR display part
What it tells you
rows: OBS / course knob
Sets the course under the index [[23:254|IFH 9-11]]
CDI needle

Centers when you are on the selected radial or its reciprocal. The edge of the center circle is 2 degrees off course and each dot adds about 2 degrees; full deflection is 12 degrees or more off course [[23:254|IFH 9-11]]
TO/FROM
Whether the selected course takes you TO or FROM the station, not which way you are pointed [[23:254|IFH 9-11]]
OFF / NAV flag
Signal too weak to use [[23:254|IFH 9-11]]

body.p: The VOR ignores your heading. It shows the same no matter where the nose points [[23:254|IFH 9-11]]. To find your radial, turn the OBS until the needle centers with FROM [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
An HSI puts the CDI on top of the heading indicator. That gives you a picture of where you are and which way you're going, and cuts workload for intercepts [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].

GPS figures distance and bearing to a waypoint and groundspeed from your position and its database [[23:269|IFH 9-26]]. It checks its own signal integrity with RAIM; without RAIM you have no assurance the position is accurate [[23:269|IFH 9-26]]. VFR and handheld GPS units are only an aid to situational awareness, not an IFR navigation source [[23:269|IFH 9-26]].

check.q: CDI needle 3 dots left. About how far off course are you?
check.a: About 8 degrees: the edge of the center circle is 2 degrees, and each dot adds about 2 more (2 + 3 x 2) [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: tune, identify, intercept, track

body.p: Buttons vary by airplane; your POH/AFM supplement has them. Generic steps, all while holding heading and altitude by instruments:

bullets: 1. Stabilize and trim the airplane first [[23:153|IFH 6-20]].
2. Tune the VOR, turn up the volume, and identify it before using it [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].
3. Orient: turn the OBS until the needle centers with FROM. That is your radial [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
4. Find the difference between the radial you want and the one you're on. Double it for the intercept angle: at least 20 degrees, no more than 90 [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
5. Set the desired course in the OBS, turn to the intercept heading, and hold it until the needle centers. Lead the turn so you don't overshoot [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
6. Track: if the needle moves left, correct left, starting with about 20 degrees. When it recenters, cut the correction in half [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
7. Set the VOR to agree with where you're going. Set to the reciprocal, it reverse-senses [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
8. When ATC gives a heading or altitude, fly it, read it back, and use the HSI heading bug as a reminder [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]] [[23:255|IFH 9-12]].

head: What the examiner wants (ACS)
Standard
rows: Control while busy
Maintain airplane control while selecting proper communications frequencies, identifying the appropriate facility, and managing navigation equipment (ACS PA.VIII.F.S1)
ATC
Comply with ATC instructions (ACS PA.VIII.F.S2)
Numbers
This Task lists no numeric tolerances; hold the heading and altitude the examiner or ATC assigns

callout.text: Load and check frequencies and the course before the hood goes on, so there is less to tune in flight. Keep charts and items neatly arranged; a disorganized flight deck can pull your eyes off the instruments long enough to enter an unusual attitude [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

check.q: You are on the 160 radial and want to intercept the 205 radial. Intercept angle?
check.a: Difference is 45 degrees; double it = 90 degrees [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

head: Facility
What it does for you
rows: Flight Service (FSS)
Briefings, flight plans, NOTAMs, weather; by radio or 1-800-WX-BRIEF [[23:55|IFH 2-4]]
Tower
Class D airspace and active runways [[23:57|IFH 2-6]]
TRACON (Approach/Departure)
Terminal radar, typically about 30 NM from the facility; sectors with their own frequencies [[23:57|IFH 2-6]]
ARTCC (Center)
En route radar; several states; same controller may use different frequencies [[23:58|IFH 2-7]]

body.p: Radar facilities give VFR aircraft basic radar service: safety alerts, traffic advisories, limited vectoring (workload permitting) and sequencing where set up [[33:218|AIM 4-1-18]]. They give vectors to VFR aircraft that can talk to them, are in radar coverage and can be radar identified [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17]].

bullets: Transponder codes come from ATC. When asked to ident, press IDENT briefly; it makes your target stand out [[23:54|IFH 2-3]].
Altitude reporting (ALT/Mode C) sends your pressure altitude; your altimeter setting doesn't change what ATC sees [[23:54|IFH 2-3]].

A safety alert means the controller sees you in unsafe proximity to terrain, obstructions or other aircraft [[33:216|AIM 4-1-16]]. Example: "Low altitude alert, check your altitude immediately" [[33:217|AIM 4-1-16]].
Vectors to a VFR pilot are advisory. Flying safely and following the regs is still your job [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17]].
Hearing "radar contact" doesn't relieve you of terrain clearance [[23:58|IFH 2-7]]. If an assigned altitude seems too low, ask before descending [[23:57|IFH 2-6]].
Keep ATC told about the weather you are in and ahead, so they don't vector you into clouds [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17]].

body.p: If your heading indicator fails, ATC can give a no-gyro vector: instead of headings, "turn right," "turn left" and "stop turn" [[34:385|AIM P/C Glossary]].

check.q: Does a radar vector to a VFR pilot authorize flying into clouds?
check.a: No. Vectors are advisory; you stay responsible for flying safely and legally [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17]].

chunks.title: When to ask for help, and using your resources

body.p: You are in at least an urgency condition the moment you are doubtful about position, fuel, weather or anything that could affect safety. That is the time to ask, not after it becomes a distress [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. Delay has cost lives [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

head: Situation
What to do
rows: Not instrument rated and can't stay VFR
Tell the controller you aren't instrument rated and declare a distress condition [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]
VFR weather route available
Take it instead of a vector or approach into IFR weather [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]
Distress
MAYDAY, preferably three times; it has priority over all other calls [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]
Urgency
PAN-PAN, three times [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]
Can't reach ATC
Lost radio

body.p: In a distress or urgency call, give as much as you need of: MAYDAY or PAN-PAN, who you're calling, call sign and type, the problem, weather, intentions and request, position and heading, altitude, fuel in minutes, and people on board [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. Then comply with instructions and ask questions if anything is unclear [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

bullets: ATC: radar assistance and vectors for a VFR aircraft in difficulty [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]], plus safety alerts [[33:216|AIM 4-1-16]].

Automation: an autopilot reduces workload and gives you time to monitor [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. A GPS nearest-airport function lists the nearest airports, up to 25 on one popular system [[23:334|IFH 11-9]].
Flight deck planning aids: charts and items arranged neatly for easy access; a messy cockpit is a distraction that leads to unusual attitudes [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].
If ATC sounds urgent and you're overloaded, it's fine to ask the controller to slow down [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

callout.text: Don't let tuning or button-pushing become the emergency. Diversion of attention while setting avionics can cause an upset [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

check.q: Lost in haze, not sure of position, not yet in danger. Which call?
check.a: Urgency: PAN-PAN. You are in an urgency condition as soon as you are doubtful about position [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]] [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].

head: Error
Fix
rows: Careless tuning and not identifying the station [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]
Tune, identify by Morse or voice, then use it
Turning the wrong way during orientation [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]
Picture your position, not your heading
Not checking TO/FROM, so reverse sensing [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]
Set the course you intend to fly
Heads-down too long while setting radios [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]
Trim, tune in short glances, return to the scan
Switching frequency without acknowledging [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3]]
Read back, then switch
Not reading back numbers or using a partial call sign [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]] [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]]
Read back altitudes, headings and runways with your full call sign
Stuck mic or wrong volume [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]]
Check volume, frequency and the mic
Accepting an instruction you can't fly safely [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]]
Say "unable" and tell ATC why

body.p: Practice: under the hood with a CFI, fly a heading and altitude while the CFI calls out frequencies to tune, stations to identify, and courses to intercept. Then add simulated ATC calls with headings and altitudes to read back and fly.

check.q: What is the most common reason for chasing a reverse-sensing needle?
check.a: Not checking the TO/FROM indicator, so the VOR is set to the reciprocal course [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

scenario.title: Flight following into lowering clouds
scenario.setup: You are a student pilot on a solo cross-country with flight following. Ceilings are lower than forecast and you lose sight of the ground in a patch of cloud. Center says: "Cessna 12345, turn right heading 090, maintain 3,500, contact Approach on 124.35." Your hand mic slips to the floor and the tablet with your frequencies has gone dark.

questions.a: Fly the airplane: wings level, trimmed, on instruments. Make a shallow turn to the heading (no more than 10 degrees of bank for a VFR pilot in IMC) [[24:367|AFH 18-18]] [[24:368|AFH 18-19]].

questions.q: How do you respond to Center?
questions.a: Read back the heading, altitude and frequency with your call sign, then switch [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]] [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3]]. If you missed something, ask right away [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123]].

questions.q: Should you go after the dropped mic?
questions.a: Not with big head movements; that invites the coriolis illusion. Retrieve things with minimal head movement or use the headset mic [[23:73|IFH 3-6]] [[23:53|IFH 2-2]].

questions.q: What do you tell Approach about your situation?
questions.a: That you are a student pilot, not instrument rated, in clouds. If you can't get back to VFR, declare a distress condition and ask for vectors to VFR weather [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].
ATC radar assistance and vectors, the autopilot if installed, and the GPS nearest-airport page [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]] [[23:219|IFH 7-58]] [[23:334|IFH 11-9]].

skills.do: Under the hood, hold heading and altitude while you select com frequencies, tune and identify a nav facility, and set up the nav display to follow a course.
skills.practice: Trim first, tune in short glances, identify every station, and use the intercept and tracking steps [[23:153|IFH 6-20]] [[23:254|IFH 9-11]] [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

skills.do: Follow ATC or examiner-simulated ATC instructions: headings, altitudes, frequency changes, squawk and ident, with correct readbacks.
skills.practice: Have your CFI play ATC; read back numbers in order with your call sign and fly them promptly [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]] [[23:54|IFH 2-3]].

quiz.q: What frequency range do civil pilots use to talk to ATC?
options: 190 to 535 kHz
quiz.why: ATC communication is on 118.000 to 136.975 MHz [[23:53|IFH 2-2]].

quiz.q: On a VOR CDI, full-scale deflection means you are at least how far off course?
options: 2 degrees
5 degrees
12 degrees
10 degrees
quiz.why: Full deflection is 12 degrees or more off course [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].

quiz.q: What does the TO/FROM indicator show?
options: Which way the nose points relative to the station you tuned
Station passage only, flagging the moment you cross over the station
Signal strength, and whether the received signal is strong enough to use
Whether the selected course leads to or from the station
quiz.why: TO/FROM shows whether the selected course, if flown, takes you TO or FROM the station [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].

quiz.q: You're on the 160 radial and want the 205 radial. What intercept angle does the IFH method give?
options: 90 degrees
45 degrees
20 degrees
135 degrees

quiz.q: Which items should you read back to ATC?
options: Only frequency changes
Altitudes, vectors and runway assignments
Altitudes printed on charted procedures
Nothing unless the controller asks
quiz.why: Read back altitude assignments, vectors and runway assignments [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]].

quiz.q: ATC tells you to change frequency. What should you do?
options: Acknowledge, then change frequency promptly
Switch without telling the controller
Wait until you reach the next fix
Stay on until ATC calls you again
quiz.why: Acknowledge the change and select the new frequency as soon as possible unless told otherwise [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3]].

quiz.q: According to the AIM, when are you in at least an urgency condition?
options: Only after an engine failure or other total loss of thrust
When you first doubt your position, fuel or weather
Only when ATC declares it for you after your position report
Only once the fuel remaining drops below 30 minutes of endurance
quiz.why: The moment you become doubtful about position, fuel endurance, weather or anything affecting safety [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

quiz.q: You've lost two-way radio communication. Which transponder code?
quiz.why: Squawk 7600 for loss of two-way radio [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]].

takeaways: Fly first. Trim, then tune in short glances.
Tune AND identify every nav station before using it.
Read back altitudes, headings and runways with your full call sign; acknowledge frequency changes.
Vectors are advisory for VFR pilots; tell ATC about the weather and that you aren't instrument rated.
Ask for help when you first feel doubt: PAN-PAN for urgency, MAYDAY for distress, 7700, 121.5.
cfi_notes: Play ATC during hood work; students often lose heading or altitude while reading back or retuning [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].
Make students orient (center with FROM) before any intercept; turning the wrong way is a classic error [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
Set the reciprocal course on purpose once so they recognize reverse sensing [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
Teach 'unable' and 'say again' as normal, safe phrases; pilots must ask when unsure [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123]].
Have them practice a MAYDAY/PAN-PAN script on the ground using the AIM 6-3-2 list [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].
gaps: The ACS Task has no numeric tolerances; the specific radios, GPS buttons and autopilot modes come from the POH/AFM supplement and avionics guides.
AFH (FAA-H-8083-3C) does not teach radio or navigation procedures; the IFH and AIM were used instead.
IFH 2-3 transponder/altitude-reporting airspace rules are older text; the lesson avoids them (current rules are in 14 CFR 91.215 and 91.225).
Navigation systems and VFR radar services are covered in more depth in lesson PA.VI.B; this lesson focuses on doing them by reference to instruments.

activities.title: True or false: radios and radio talk

cards.s: If ATC gives you a frequency your radio can't tune, stay on the old one and wait.
cards.why: No. Ask ATC for an alternative frequency [[23:53|IFH 2-2]].

cards.s: Switching the audio panel from COM1 to COM2 changes what you hear as well as what you send.
cards.why: Yes. The switch changes both the transmitter and the receiver [[23:54|IFH 2-3]].

cards.s: After you change to a new frequency, pause and listen before you talk.
cards.why: Yes. Make sure the frequency is clear first [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]].

cards.s: On first contact with a new controller, "Cessna Three Four Five" is fine instead of your full call sign.
cards.why: No. Never shorten your call sign on initial contact [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]].

cards.s: Read back headings and altitudes in the same order the controller gave them.
cards.why: Yes, and include your call sign [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]] [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]].

cards.s: Keep it brief, so use only short standard phrases even if the controller may not understand you.
cards.why: No. Understanding comes first. Use whatever words it takes to get your message across [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1]].

activities.title: Read the VOR display
activities.intro: Tap what the VOR shows, then what it means.

pairs.r: You are on the 090 radial; flying 270 takes you to the station

pairs.l: Needle swings fast side to side
pairs.r: You are close to the station

pairs.l: OBS set to the reciprocal course
pairs.r: Reverse sensing: corrections go the wrong way

pairs.l: Needle drifts slowly left on course
pairs.r: Crosswind from the left; correct left about 20 degrees

activities.title: Intercept a VOR course
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Trim the airplane so it holds heading and altitude while you look away
Tune the VOR and identify it by Morse code or voice
Center the needle with FROM to find your radial
Double the difference between radials for the intercept angle
Turn the OBS to the course you want
Turn to the intercept heading and hold it
As the needle centers, turn onto the course and track it

activities.title: PAN-PAN or MAYDAY?
activities.intro: Tap a situation, then tap the call it needs.

items.t: Not sure where you are, but not in danger yet
A fire in the engine compartment
Doubtful your fuel will last to the airport
Not instrument rated, in cloud, can't get back to VFR
A mechanical failure, like the engine quitting

final_quiz.q: You are under the hood holding 3,500 feet when ATC asks you to tune a new frequency. What should you make sure of before you look down at the radio?
options: That you have told ATC you are a student pilot and are flying under the hood
That the OBS is set to the course you want and the CDI needle is centered
That the cabin speaker is turned up high enough to hear ATC while you tune
That the airplane is trimmed to hold its attitude while you glance away
final_quiz.why: Good trim lets you relax pressure on the yoke and turn your attention to another task for a moment without leaving the attitude [[23:153|IFH 6-20]]. Then tune in short glances and go back to the scan.

final_quiz.q: You want flight following from Albany Approach. Your airplane is Cessna 12345. Which first call fits the AIM format?
options: Albany Approach, Cessna One Two Three Four Five, request V-F-R traffic advisories.
Cessna Three Four Five, requesting V-F-R traffic advisories from Albany Approach.
Requesting V-F-R traffic advisories, Albany Approach, this is Cessna Three Four Five.
Cessna One Two Three Four Five, with you at 3,500, requesting V-F-R flight following.
final_quiz.why: Initial contact is the facility name, then your full call sign, then your request [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3]]. Never shorten your call sign on initial contact [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]].

final_quiz.q: ATC says: "Cessna One Two Three Four Five, turn left heading 180, descend and maintain 3,000." Which readback is best?
options: Roger, Cessna One Two Three Four Five.
Descend and maintain 3,000, left heading 180, Cessna One Two Three Four Five.
Left heading 180, descend and maintain 3,000.
Left heading 180, descend and maintain 3,000, Cessna One Two Three Four Five.
final_quiz.why: Read back headings and altitudes in the same order ATC gave them, and include your call sign [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]] [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]]. A plain "roger" doesn't check the numbers.

final_quiz.q: Approach gives you an altitude, but static covers part of it. You think it was 4,500, but you aren't sure. What should you do?
options: Climb to 4,500 and read it back later
Stay quiet and wait for ATC to repeat it
Ask ATC to say it again right away
Pick an altitude that keeps you clear of clouds and report it
final_quiz.why: A pilot who is unsure of an ATC clearance must ask ATC to clarify it immediately [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]]. Guessing at a number is how readback errors start.

final_quiz.q: You tune and identify a VOR, then turn the OBS until the needle centers. The OBS reads 045 with FROM showing. Where are you?
options: On the 225 radial, southwest of the station
On the 045 radial, northeast of the station
Heading 045, flying toward the station
On the 045 radial, but only if your heading is 045
final_quiz.why: With the needle centered and FROM showing, the OBS index shows the radial you are on [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]. The VOR ignores heading; it shows the same no matter where the nose points [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].

final_quiz.q: You are on the 100 radial and want to intercept the 105 radial. Using the IFH method, what intercept angle should you use?
options: 5 degrees
10 degrees
20 degrees
45 degrees
final_quiz.why: The difference is 5 degrees. Doubled, that is 10, but the IFH says the intercept angle is never less than 20 degrees or more than 90, so use 20 [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

final_quiz.q: You are tracking a course of 270 to a VOR. The needle drifted left, so you turned to heading 250. Now the needle is centered again. What heading should you try next?
final_quiz.why: Start with about a 20 degree correction toward the needle. When the needle centers again, cut the correction in half: 20 becomes 10, so heading 260 [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

final_quiz.q: You are flying outbound from a VOR on the 090 radial, heading about 090, but you left the OBS set to 270. What happens when you correct toward the needle?
options: The needle reverse-senses, taking you farther off course
Nothing changes; the VOR works the same either way you set the OBS
The OFF flag appears until you reset the OBS to the correct course
The needle swings fast and the flag changes, showing you have passed the station
final_quiz.why: Set to the reciprocal of your course, the CDI reverse-senses and corrections go the wrong way. Set the OBS to agree with the course you intend to fly, here 090 [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

final_quiz.q: You are VFR with flight following. Approach gives you a heading that points at a cloud bank ahead. What should you do?
options: Fly the heading; ATC is responsible for keeping you out of clouds
Fly the heading; a vector makes it legal to enter the cloud
Turn off your transponder and turn away without a word
Tell Approach about the clouds and ask for a different heading
final_quiz.why: Vectors to VFR pilots are advisory, and flying safely and legally is still your job. Keep the controller told about the weather ahead [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17]]. Accepting or refusing an instruction is your call [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]].

final_quiz.q: Before takeoff you set the wrong altimeter setting by mistake. What altitude does Approach see from your transponder's altitude reporting?
options: Your indicated altitude, including the error from the wrong setting
Your pressure altitude, whatever the altimeter is set to
Nothing at all, until you fix the altimeter setting and the unit resets
Your height above the ground, from the radar return of your airplane
final_quiz.why: With the transponder in ALT, it sends your pressure altitude. Changing the altimeter setting has no effect on the altitude the controller reads [[23:54|IFH 2-3]].

final_quiz.q: Approach says: "Low altitude alert, Cessna One Two Three Four Five, check your altitude immediately." What does this tell you?
options: The controller sees you possibly too close to terrain or obstructions
You have climbed above your assigned altitude and must descend back to it right now
Your transponder has stopped reporting altitude and must be reset at once
Another pilot has reported you to ATC for flying below the minimum altitude
final_quiz.why: A safety alert means the controller judges your altitude puts you in unsafe proximity to terrain, obstructions or other aircraft. What to do about it is your decision [[33:216|AIM 4-1-16]]. Controllers spot low altitude mainly from your Mode C reports [[33:217|AIM 4-1-16]].

final_quiz.q: You have flight following across a large rural area. As you fly from one area to the next, the same controller keeps giving you new frequencies. Which facility are you most likely talking to?
options: Tower
Flight Service
Center (ARTCC)
Approach (TRACON)
final_quiz.why: Each Center covers several states through remote radio sites, so you may hear the same controller on different frequencies [[23:58|IFH 2-7]]. Approach airspace normally reaches only about 30 NM from its facility [[23:57|IFH 2-6]].

final_quiz.q: You are a student pilot. Clouds have closed in around you and there is no way to get back to VFR. What does the AIM say to tell ATC?
options: Ask for an instrument approach and say nothing about your rating
Say you are not instrument rated, and declare a distress condition
Ask for an IFR clearance
Say you will climb on top of the clouds and stay VFR
final_quiz.why: A pilot without an instrument rating who can't continue in VFR conditions should tell the controller so and declare a distress condition [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]. Asking for an IFR clearance is only for an instrument-rated, current pilot in an equipped airplane [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

final_quiz.q: You are making a MAYDAY call. How does the AIM say to report your fuel?
options: In gallons remaining
In pounds remaining
In minutes remaining
As a percent of full tanks
final_quiz.why: A distress or urgency message includes fuel remaining in minutes, along with your position, altitude and the number of people on board [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].
